records.title: Rapid Bilateral Ocular Metastasis of Feline Injection-Site Sarcoma Despite Early Radical Therapeutic Intervention.
records.abstract: To report on clinical, ophthalmic, and pathologic features of a rare case of bilateral ocular metastasis of feline injection-site sarcoma despite early radical therapeutic intervention. A 6-year-old female spayed domestic shorthair cat with the complaint of a left hindlimb mass 10 months following vaccination. Initial fine needle aspirate of mass was suggestive of sarcoma. Following staging that was within normal limits, amputation of limb was performed. A high-grade sarcoma was confirmed histologically, with complete excision. Three weeks postoperatively, the patient developed ataxia, left-sided mydriasis, and panuveitis with papilledema and partial retinal separation. Thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound revealed multifocal pulmonary, splenic, renal, jejunal, and lymph node masses consistent with metastatic neoplasia. The cat declined rapidly and was euthanized approximately 10 weeks after initial presentation. Necropsy confirmed widespread metastatic fibrosarcoma involving multiple organs and both eyes. Histopathology demonstrated intravascular neoplastic spindle cells within the choroid and peripapillary connective tissue bilaterally, consistent with hematogenous ocular metastasis. This case showcases an unusually aggressive FISS with bilateral ocular metastases developing only weeks following surgical removal. Despite histologically complete excision, rapid systemic dissemination occurred, highlighting the potential for early micrometastasis. Ocular and neurologic signs may serve as early indicators of metastatic spread in FISS, emphasizing the need for vigilant postoperative monitoring and adjunctive therapeutic consideration.

records.title: Iatrogenic rectal perforation in two cats secondary to use of a faecal loop.
records.abstract: Two male, neutered, Domestic Shorthair cats, aged 5 and 8 years, were presented to the University of Florida for evaluation and correction of rectal perforations that occurred during faecal sample collection with faecal loops at their primary care hospitals. One cat presented with a fever, neutropenia, and lymphocytosis, while the other had a fever, thrombocytopenia, hyperglycaemia, and was approximately 5% dehydrated. In both cases, radiography identified a heterogeneous soft tissue and gas opacity adjacent to the rectum, and CT scans identified a defect in the rectal wall with associated pocketing, subcutaneous faecal material, and subcutaneous emphysema. The rectal defects were repaired surgically in both cats using a lateral perineal approach. Both surgical sites were treated with open wound management and left to heal by second intention. Iatrogenic rectal perforation. There are risks associated with the use of instruments, such as faecal loops or thermometers, in the rectum. Associated trauma can lead to potentially life-threatening complications. Early detection of rectal perforation is vital to reduce further complications and improve clinical outcomes.

records.title: An intrauterine grass awn foreign body in a dog.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: A 3-year-old intact female West Highland white terrier dog with a history of acute lethargy and diarrhea was presented to the University of Calgary's Diagnostic Services Unit (Calgary, Alberta) for a postmortem examination. Necropsy and subsequent histopathologic examination revealed suppurative peritonitis and ulcerative metritis with an intraluminal grass awn foreign body. Bacterial culture identified  Escherichia coli  and  Streptococcus lutetiensis  in the uterus and spleen. Sudden death was attributed to septic shock secondary to the uterine infection. This case highlighted the rare but clinically important condition of intrauterine grass awn foreign body in a dog. Key clinical message: This case illustrates that migrating plant material can, uncommonly, enter the canine uterus and induce severe inflammatory disease, including metritis, and should be considered among differential diagnoses for uterine pathology.

records.title: Peracute infectious canine hepatitis in a Canadian puppy.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: Infectious canine hepatitis (ICH), caused by canine adenovirus type 1 (CAV-1), is now rare in Canada due to vaccination, though sporadic and severe cases still occur. This report describes the peracute presentation, diagnostic findings, and management challenges of an 11-week-old German shepherd mix dog with ICH complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The puppy was presented with lethargy, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, abdominal pain and effusion, and progressive shock of duration < 24 h. Point-of-care ultrasound showed marked abdominal effusion, and diagnostic testing revealed severe thrombocytopenia, prolonged clotting times, hypoproteinemia, elevated liver enzymes, hyperbilirubinemia, metabolic acidosis, and hyperlactatemia, consistent with acute hepatic failure and DIC. Despite aggressive supportive care, the dog deteriorated within 4 h and was euthanized. Postmortem histopathological and PCR assessment confirmed CAV-1 hepatic necrosis and ICH. This case highlights the continued presence of CAV-1 in Canada, including likely urban exposure, and reinforces the need for vaccination. This report also underscores the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of peracute ICH with secondary DIC, in which early intervention may influence outcome. Key clinical message: Peracute ICH, though rare in vaccinated populations, remains a fatal differential diagnosis in young dogs presented with acute collapse and hepatic failure, even in urban environments. In addition, the continued presence of this disease reinforces the importance of vaccination and helps inform future vaccination recommendations for rescue groups and independent owners.

records.title: Cervical vertebral osteomyelitis mimicking neoplasia in a dog: Successful surgical management and diagnostic challenges.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: A 10-year-old male mixed-breed dog weighing ~15 kg was presented with chronic cervical pain and progressive neurological deficits. Computed tomography revealed severe osteolysis of the C4 vertebral body and a contrast-enhancing extradural lesion causing marked spinal cord compression; these findings were highly suggestive of neoplasia. Due to neurological deterioration, surgical intervention was conducted. The dog underwent a subtotal lateral corpectomy followed by asymmetric stabilization using monoaxial vertebral screws and titanium rods. Intraoperative findings revealed friable tissue and extensive bone destruction suggestive of infection rather than neoplasia. Bacterial culture yielded  Staphylococcus aureus  susceptible to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, whereas fungal culture was negative. Histopathological assessment demonstrated inflammatory changes without evidence of neoplasia. The dog showed rapid clinical improvement following surgery and culture-guided antimicrobial therapy (amoxicillin-clavulanic acid: 15 mg/kg, PO, q12h for 45 d). The dog was discharged 24 h after surgery and remained pain-free with no evidence of recurrence over a follow-up period of at least 2 y. Key clinical message: This case highlights the diagnostic challenges associated with vertebral lesions that mimic neoplasia and emphasizes the role of surgical intervention in both diagnosis and treatment.

records.title: Erosive immune-mediated polyarthritis in 4 Maltese dogs.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: The medical records of a veterinary teaching hospital were retrospectively reviewed between 2021 and 2024 and 4 Maltese dogs with erosive immune-mediated polyarthritis were identified. Signalment, physical examination findings, radiographic findings, synovial fluid analysis, medical treatments, and outcome for each affected Maltese dog was recorded. A dog was classified as having erosive immunemediated polyarthritis if radiographic evidence of erosive arthritis was endorsed by a Board-certified radiologist. Fourteen dogs were diagnosed with idiopathic immune-mediated polyarthritis, of which 4 (28.6%) met the criteria for erosive immune-mediated polyarthritis; all were of the Maltese breed. On admission, affected dogs were presented with lameness, deformation, and swelling of the carpal joints. Radiographs revealed bone lytic lesions; synovial fluid analysis indicated suppurative, non-septic polyarthritis. Three dogs received combination immunosuppressive therapy, resulting in complete remission in 1 dog and partial remission in 2 dogs. Key clinical message: The present report highlights a cluster of erosive immune-mediated polyarthritis in Maltese dogs and may indicate a breed predisposition towards erosive arthropathies. This case series also demonstrates the challenges of treating this disease, as immunosuppressive treatment appeared to uncommonly lead to full clinical remission, with only 1 dog achieving complete cytologic remission. Joint deformation was not improved in any of the dogs.

records.title: Bilateral  Brucella -associated septic hip arthritis in a dog.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: A 3-year-old spayed female mixed-breed dog was evaluated for bilateral pelvic-limb lameness and abnormal gait. Radiographic and computed tomographic examination revealed bilateral coxofemoral joint arthritis and discospondylitis. Serologic testing using indirect fluorescent antibody and agar gel immunodiffusion confirmed  Brucella canis  infection. The dog was treated with oral doxycycline and enrofloxacin for 1 y, until  Brucella  polymerase chain reaction was negative. Palliative bilateral femoral head and neck excisions were carried out, and resolution of clinical pelvic-limb lameness was documented. Vertebral involvement, including discospondylitis and sacroiliitis, has been previously documented in canine brucellosis. However, hip joint involvement, although it is a recognized manifestation in human brucellosis, has not been previously reported in the veterinary literature. Key clinical message:  Brucella canis  should be considered as a differential diagnosis in dogs with septic hip arthritis, especially when multiple joints and vertebrae are affected.

records.title: Multimodal management of refractory cutaneous nocardiosis in a feline immunodeficiency virus-positive cat.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: A 7-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat positive for feline immunodeficiency virus was presented with a 2-year history of recurrent ulcerative cutaneous lesions on the dorsum. Microbiological identification revealed  Nocardia nova , and histopathological findings were consistent with cutaneous nocardiosis. Systemic minocycline was selected based on antimicrobial susceptibility testing, but long-term administration was limited by gastrointestinal adverse effects. Because prolonged systemic antimicrobial therapy could not be maintained, local adjunctive therapies, including topical amikacin in tris-EDTA, amikacin-loaded 30% poloxamer 407, and cold atmospheric microwave plasma, were used to support lesion control but did not achieve complete resolution. Surgical excision was directed at the persistent main lesion and an adjacent lesion associated with extensive subcutaneous dead space. Complete healing was achieved, with no recurrence during an 11-month postoperative follow-up period. Key clinical message: Systemic antimicrobial therapy guided by culture and susceptibility testing remains the cornerstone of treatment for feline cutaneous nocardiosis. Adjunctive local therapies may support lesion control when systemic therapy is poorly tolerated, but timely surgical excision should be considered when persistent, localized lesions are associated with chronic fibrotic tissue or subcutaneous dead space.

records.title: Insidious eunatremic, eukalemic primary hypoadrenocorticism in a dog.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: A 10-year-old spayed female papillon dog with alopecia underwent an ACTH stimulation test to rule out hyperadrenocorticism. The results unexpectedly revealed primary hypoadrenocorticism characterized by increased endogenous ACTH concentration in conjunction with a subnormal cortisol response. Plasma electrolyte concentrations were within normal limits, though low post-ACTH aldosterone concentrations were subsequently identified. Congenital/juvenile hypoadrenocorticism had been ruled out  via  previous ACTH response testing in the workup of chronic diarrhea at 1 y of age. No treatment for hypoadrenocorticism was given initially. Over the next 3 y, glucocorticoid function gradually declined, electrolyte concentrations remained within normal limits, and alopecia resolved. The dog had a subsequent hypoglucocorticoid crisis associated with pancreatitis at 13 y age, after which prednisolone treatment was started. Dosage was adjusted over time based on endogenous ACTH and aldosterone concentrations and plasma renin activity when possible. The dog's hypocortisolemia was acceptably controlled for the next 2 y. Plasma electrolyte concentrations continued to remain within normal limits, without mineralocorticoid replacement, until the dog ultimately died from congestive heart failure associated with myxomatous mitral valve disease. Severe bilateral trizonal cortical adrenal atrophy and mild lymphoplasmacytic adrenalitis were identified on necropsy. Key clinical message: This report documents insidious atypical Addison's disease in a dog with a preclinical course of > 3 y and clinical course of 2 y. Although all 3 zones of the adrenal cortex were destroyed, plasma electrolyte concentrations remained within normal limits.

records.title: Exertional syncope caused by acquired obstruction of the pulmonary artery due to an organized thrombus in a dog.
records.abstract: An 8.5-year-old Boxer was referred for evaluation of frequently occurring exercise-induced seizure-like episodes for 2.5 months. Cardiac auscultation revealed a left basilar systolic murmur with an intensity of IV/VI. Echocardiography showed severe pulmonary arterial obstruction with a pressure gradient of 90 mmHg due to a suspected intraluminal mass. Cardiac catheterization was performed, where a right ventriculogram revealed a large rounded filling defect in the pulmonary artery trunk. No balloon angioplasty, biopsy or stenting were attempted. After euthanasia, post-mortem examination revealed an organized thrombus of unknown etiology attached to the wall of the pulmonary artery trunk. The adjacent arterial wall showed a markedly thickened intimal layer. The etiology remains unclear, primarily due to the chronic nature of the condition. Antemortem blood tests and postmortem examination failed to reveal any prothrombotic conditions. Acquired causes of pulmonary arterial obstruction are extremely rare in dogs, and an organized thrombus has not been reported yet.

records.title: Sex steroids in animals absent gonads: A case series.
records.abstract: Identifying possible sources of sex steroids is challenging in animals exhibiting apparent responses in reproductive tissues but presenting with a history of having been neutered. Sex steroids, typically secreted by the gonads, also induce responses in non-reproductive tissues including the skin or brain, sometimes affecting behaviors. The analysis of hormones has become a mainstay of diagnostic endocrinology in small and large animal practice. The repertoire of those with reproductive relevance has expanded significantly with specific immunoassays detecting anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) from either ovarian granulosa or testicular Sertoli cells. This has proven to be extremely useful differentiating neutered animals from those that are not. When AMH is undetectable, indicating neutered status, the possibility of sex steroid secretion by non-gonadal, pathological tissue, or other exogenous sources becomes very real. Reported gonadal status (as stated by owners) is not always reliable given that changes of ownership are common, and neutering is not always complete, complicating initial diagnosis. The cases reported here include several that are unique in either their presentation, diagnostic approach or likely etiologic origin. All were submitted primarily for an assessment of their gonadal status. Collectively, they illustrate, with unusual insight, the utility of AMH as a gonadal biomarker, while obviating the complexity of interpretation of reproductive hormone analyses in supposedly gonadectomized cats, horses and dogs manifesting a variety of apparent, reproductive conditions and pathologies.

records.title: Ecological Implications of Rodenticide Exposure: First Evidence of Bromadiolone Poisoning in an Indian Leopard ( Panthera pardus fusca ).
records.abstract: Large carnivores such as Indian leopard ( Panthera pardus fusca ) play a crucial role in maintaining ecosystem stability. However, they face increasing threats from habitat loss and other anthropogenic pressures. One significant but underreported threat is unintentional or deliberate poisoning, particularly from chemical pesticides. This study reports the first documented case of rodenticide (bromadiolone) poisoning in a large mammalian carnivore in India. In this study, a deceased female leopard (~5 years old) was recovered from the Nilgiris Forest Division, Tamil Nadu, India. Tissues of kidney, liver, and gut contents of the leopard were collected for toxicological investigation. Using high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), the samples were screened for 51 pesticides. Bromadiolone, a second-generation anticoagulant rodenticide (SGAR), was detected at concentrations of 802.9 ng/g in kidney, 237.7 ng/g in liver, and 39.3 ng/g in gut. No other pesticides were detected in any of the samples studied. Postmortem examination revealed internal hemorrhaging consistent with bromadiolone-induced coagulopathy, confirming it as the likely cause of death. This study underscores the ecological risk posed by rodenticides through deliberate or secondary poisoning of nontarget wildlife. To prevent such incidents, stricter regulations and greater public awareness regarding the use of anticoagulant rodenticides near forested areas are urgently needed. Additionally, long-term monitoring and research on rodenticide exposure are strongly recommended to guide further conservation actions and safeguard wildlife across the country.

records.title: Histopathological observation and diagnosis of hepatic neuroendocrine carcinoma in a cat.
records.abstract: Hepatic neuroendocrine carcinoma is a rare hepatic neoplasm in cats. It is generally considered highly malignant with a poor prognosis. Therefore, early diagnosis and appropriate treatment of such tumors are critical for a successful outcome. This report describes a 6-year-old male Oriental Longhair cat presented to our hospital with a primary complaint of recurrent vomiting and mild abdominal distension. Ultrasonography revealed heterogeneous echogenicity of the hepatic parenchyma, indicating uneven hepatic density. Laparotomy revealed white and dark red nodules of varying sizes on the liver surface. Histopathological examination showed that the hepatic mass was composed of malignant neoplastic cells with typical neuroendocrine differentiation features. Immunohistochemical staining for CgA and NSE confirmed that the liver tumor cells were derived from the neuroendocrine system. Following histopathological diagnosis, the cat received palliative treatment and died 34 days after the initial presentation. Through histopathological observation and diagnosis of feline hepatic neuroendocrine carcinoma, this study provides a useful reference for the future clinical diagnosis of this disease.

records.title: Surgical repair of an ostium secundum atrial septal defect with absent dorsal rim in a dog.
records.abstract: To describe the anatomical characteristics and surgical practicality of repairing an ostium secundum atrial septal defect (ASD), lacking a dorsal rim, in a dog. Case report. A 1-year-old, 4.7 kg spayed female Bichon Frise dog presenting with exercise intolerance and cough. Clinical data, including diagnostic imaging studies, surgical records, and postoperative follow-up findings, were reviewed. The dog underwent open-heart repair under cardiopulmonary bypass using a glutaraldehyde-fixed autologous pericardial patch, with the rim-deficient dorsal portion anchored to the atrial free wall. The dog recovered uneventfully from surgery, and the closed defect remained stable during a 406 days follow-up period. No peri- or postoperative complications were observed. Surgical closure of a secundum ASD lacking a dorsal rim was successfully achieved using an autologous pericardial patch, resulting in stable defect repair without complications during follow-up.

records.title: Computed tomographic features and clinical outcome of a presumed subconjunctival hibernoma in a dog.
records.journal: The Journal of small animal practice
records.abstract: An 11-year-old male neutered German shepherd dog was presented for evaluation of a left subconjunctival mass associated with mild exophthalmos and ventral globe deviation. CT identified a well-defined, contrast-enhancing, soft tissue attenuating mass within the dorsal subconjunctival region. The mass was removed via globe-sparing excisional biopsy after it was found intraoperatively to be discrete and readily separable from surrounding tissues. Histopathology identified an adipocytic neoplasm most consistent with hibernoma, although liposarcoma could not be definitively excluded. No clinically apparent local tumour recurrence was identified on general physical examination 18 months postoperatively. This report provides CT characterisation of a presumed subconjunctival hibernoma together with globe-sparing excision and long-term clinical follow-up.

records.title: Primary diffuse meningeal melanomatosis in a dog: Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings.
records.abstract: Primary diffuse meningeal melanomatosis is a rare neoplasm in dogs that arises from leptomeningeal melanocytes of neural crest origin. This report describes the clinicopathological and immunohistochemical features of a primary diffuse meningeal melanomatosis in a 10-year-old female spayed Staffordshire Bull Terrier that presented with progressive neurological dysfunction, including blindness and seizures. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed moderate mononuclear pleocytosis. Histologically, a densely cellular, poorly demarcated and infiltrative neoplasm multifocally expanded the leptomeninges overlying the cerebrum and cerebellum and invaded the adjacent neuroparenchyma. Neoplastic cells were arranged in sheets, cords and solid aggregates, polygonal to spindle-shaped and occasionally contained intracytoplasmic, brown granular pigment consistent with melanin. Immunohistochemically, neoplastic cells exhibited moderate diffuse nuclear immunoreactivity for SOX10 and moderate cytoplasmic labelling for Melan A, supporting melanocytic differentiation. Based on morphological features, the invasive growth pattern and immunophenotype, a diagnosis of primary diffuse meningeal melanomatosis was established. No extracranial primary melanoma was identified at postmortem examination. From a comparative perspective, this case mirrors the spectrum of primary central nervous system melanocytic tumours recognised in human neuropathology, where the exclusion of metastatic disease is essential, and histological features such as mitotic activity and parenchymal invasion correlate with biological behaviour.

records.title: Presumed Leflunomide-Induced Lung Injury in a Dog.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)
records.abstract: To describe a clinical case of presumed drug-induced lung disease (DILD) caused by leflunomide, including a clinical case summary and a discussion of current veterinary and translational understandings of the diagnostic and therapeutic approach to DILD and the possible relationship between leflunomide use and interstitial lung disease in a dog. A 1-year-old intact male mixed-breed dog with a history of steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis managed on prednisone, leflunomide, and cyclosporine was presented for a 2-day history of coughing, vomiting, lethargy, and anorexia. Thoracic radiographs showed an interstitial pulmonary pattern, while computed tomography showed diffuse pulmonary infiltrates and severe tracheobronchial lymphadenomegaly. Diagnostic testing including fungal serology and airway cytology/culture effectively ruled out infectious etiologies. Because the patient responded completely to a cessation of leflunomide therapy and anti-inflammatory doses of corticosteroids, we suspect these signs were the result of DILD as has been reported with leflunomide use in people. This is the first report of leflunomide-induced lung disease in veterinary medicine. Clinicians should be aware of the adverse drug event and use caution when considering this medication in patients with preexisting pulmonary disease.

records.title: Cystic clear cell thymoma in a cat: clinical, imaging, anatomopathological and immunohistochemical findings.
records.abstract: Thymomas are uncommon thymic epithelial neoplasms in cats and may present uncommon histological variants, such as cystic clear cell thymoma. The aim of this case report was to describe the clinical, imaging, anatomopathological, and immunohistochemical findings of a cystic clear cell thymoma in a four-year-old mixed-breed female cat presented with anorexia and progressive dyspnea. Imaging examinations revealed a large heterogeneous mediastinal mass with cystic components, accompanied by pleural effusion and pulmonary compression. Ultrasound-guided cytology was inconclusive. Despite intensive supportive care, the patient died due to respiratory failure. Necropsy revealed a large mediastinal mass occupying approximately 70-80% of the thoracic cavity, accompanied by compressive pulmonary atelectasis and hydrothorax. Histologically, the neoplasm was predominantly composed of carbohydrate-rich clear epithelial cells accompanied by cystic structures, scattered mature lymphocytes and rare Hassall's corpuscles. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong nuclear expression of p40, p63 and CKAE1/AE3 in the neoplastic cells, whereas CD3 labeling was restricted to non-neoplastic lymphocytes, supporting the diagnosis of cystic clear cell thymoma. This report expands the current knowledge of this rare tumor variant in cats and highlights the importance of imaging examinations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry for establishing a definitive diagnosis.

records.title: Description of a transtemporal surgical approach to the mandibular coronoid process region in two dogs with oral pain.
records.journal: The Journal of small animal practice
records.abstract: Conditions affecting the mandibular coronoid process and surgical approaches to it are rarely described in veterinary medicine. We describe and illustrate an alternative surgical approach to the mandibular coronoid process in two dogs. Two dogs presented with a chronic history of pain while opening the mouth. Computed tomography identified unilateral contrast-enhancing soft tissues around the proximal mandibular coronoid process. The mandibular coronoid process in each dog was approached via a transtemporal muscular approach dorsal to the zygomatic arch, without the need for a zygomatic osteotomy. This allowed access to both the proximal medial and lateral aspects of the mandibular coronoid process. A foreign body was surgically identified in one case, whereas no foreign material was retrieved in the other. Both dogs were free of clinical signs up to 6 months postoperatively. The described technique provided a less invasive approach, resulting in reduced tissue damage, reduced postoperative pain and rapid recovery.

records.title: Suspected Incidental Release of Cardiac Tamponade From Chest Compressions in a Dog.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)
records.abstract: To describe the clinical presentation, management, and outcome of a dog with suspected pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade that may have been released with chest compressions during CPR. A dog was presented to a primary care veterinarian for dyspnea. Thoracic radiographs showed a globoid cardiac silhouette and no pleural effusion. The dog was transferred immediately to a referral veterinary hospital and was unresponsive and pulseless on arrival. Chest compressions were commenced as part of CPR, and return of spontaneous circulation was achieved. Thoracic radiographs after return of spontaneous circultation showed a more normal-appearing cardiac silhouette and new pleural effusion. An echocardiogram showed a right auricular mass. The dog died at home approximately 48 h after initial presentation. This report describes the first known case of suspected incidental release of cardiac tamponade temporally associated with chest compressions in a dog.

records.title: Acute Tracheal Narrowing due to Suspected Intramural Tracheal Hemorrhage in a Dog With Hemophilia A.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)
records.abstract: To describe a case of spontaneous intramural tracheal hemorrhage with subsequent tracheal narrowing leading to a respiratory crisis in a dog with hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency). The dog had a known history of hemophilia A and had been evaluated at a different facility the day prior, where thoracic radiographs showed severe tracheal attenuation, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of tracheal collapse. Intramural tracheal hemorrhage can present similarly to tracheal collapse and is a differential for tracheal narrowing on radiographs. There have been previous reports of dogs in respiratory distress with tracheal narrowing due to hemorrhage caused by anticoagulant rodenticide toxicosis. This is the first case report documenting spontaneous hemorrhage secondary to hemophilia A causing tracheal narrowing. Although rare, hemorrhage should be considered in all cases of tracheal narrowing, especially in patients without a chronic history of cough and those that fail to respond to standard treatment for tracheal collapse. Dogs with a known diagnosis of hemophilia A should be assumed to have bleeding almost regardless of their clinical presentation and treated accordingly.

records.title: Gastric ulcers in cats with feline infectious peritonitis.
records.abstract: Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is one of the leading causes of death in cats worldwide. Although multiple organs can be affected, gastric ulcers have not been previously described as part of the pathological picture. The affected cats had multisystemic involvement and the disease was classified as three mixed and one non-effusive case of FIP. Gross changes in the stomach were identified in all cases and consisted of single or multiple ulcers of variable diameter that were surrounded by a hyperemic halo. Histologically, ulcerated lesions consisted of areas of mucosal loss with coagulative necrosis surrounded by fibrin and cellular debris and, in some cases, pyogranulomatous inflammation. In the submucosa there was pyogranulomatous vasculitis, thrombosis, and fibrinoid vascular necrosis. All cases had positive immunolabeling for FCoV in the cytoplasm of macrophages within the gastric mucosa and submucosa. Although ulcerative gastritis is not a classic manifestation of FIP, the vasculitis and thrombosis observed in these cases likely contributed to the development of gastric ulcers. FIP should be considered as a differential diagnosis in cats with gastric ulcers associated with pyogranulomatous inflammatory infiltrate.

records.title: Acute Exercise-Associated Collapse in a Racing Siberian Husky: A Case Report.
records.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
records.abstract: The cause of exercise-associated collapse is rarely established when episodes are transient and occur in the field. A 4.5-year-old intact female Siberian Husky with a body condition score of 3/9 collapsed while competing in a 246 km multi-stage sled-dog race at about 1500 m altitude. On day 2, after 14 min of running and at the start of the first uphill section, she fell into lateral recumbency, became apnoeic and unresponsive, and recovered within seconds after chest compressions by the musher. Investigations comprised clinical examination, blood analyses at 30 min and 72 h, dietary analysis, training records and race tracking data. The examination 10 min later was unremarkable. Hyperglycaemia, increased cortisol and muscle and liver enzyme activities, and a mildly decreased haematocrit were consistent with an acute exercise and stress response. Calculated energy intake (1633 kcal/day) was below estimated racing requirements (2116-2539 kcal/day), and she had trained almost exclusively on flat terrain near sea level. No definitive cause could be identified. Several contributing factors were considered, including body condition, nutritional status, training specificity, altitude exposure, and race demands. A transient mismatch between oxygen delivery and metabolic demand remains one possible explanation; however, this hypothesis could not be confirmed, and a transient cardiac arrhythmia could not be excluded. Unexplained collapse in canine endurance athletes warrants withdrawal from competition and a structured cardiovascular, metabolic, nutritional, and training evaluation.

records.title: Electrochemotherapy for urinary bladder botryoid rhabdomyosarcoma in a dog: case report.
records.abstract: Urinary bladder rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is a rare malignant neoplasm in dogs, most commonly affecting young animals and frequently arising from the trigone region, where complete surgical removal is challenging. records.abstract: To describe the clinical features and successful surgical management of a giant, symptomatic urachal cyst (UC) in a dog using a laparoscopic-assisted approach without partial cystectomy. The patient remained clinically well, and no recurrence was noted during a 20-month follow-up. records.title: Multiple cartilaginous exostosis in a feline: Case report.
records.abstract: Multiple cartilaginous exostoses (MCE), or osteochondromatosis, is a benign neoplasm characterized by the presence of nodules on the bone surface. The animal presented with cachexia, hyporexia, dehydration, and increased bone volume in multiple anatomical regions. Radiographic examination revealed proliferative sclerotic lesions, and histopathology confirmed osteochondrogenic proliferation consistent with MCE. Initial treatment included doxycycline and prednisolone. After 30 days, the cat showed clinical improvement; however, the osseous proliferations continued to increase in size. Subsequent radiographic evaluation demonstrated marked lesion progression, accompanied by worsening clinical signs. Due to the extent of the lesions and the unfavorable clinical condition, euthanasia was elected. This report highlights the clinical and imaging features of MCE in a young FeLV-positive cat and emphasizes the importance of early diagnosis and imaging follow-up in the management of affected patients.

records.journal: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)
records.abstract: To describe the clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of hypocalcemia secondary to inadvertent administration of denosumab in a 4-month-old kitten. A 4-month-old neutered female domestic shorthair kitten was presented with acute weakness, tremors, third eyelid prolapse, and ataxia for several hours. Physical examination revealed lethargy, tachycardia, hypothermia, mild dehydration, and apparent nausea. Neurologic findings included tremors, cerebellar ataxia, bilateral mydriasis, and decreased bilateral direct and indirect pupillary reflexes. ECG confirmed sinus tachycardia. Blood work showed severe ionized hypocalcemia (0.74 mmol/L [2.96 mg/dL]; reference interval [RI]: 1.10-1.40 [4.40-5.60]), mild hypokalemia (3.38 mmol/L [3.38 mEq/L]; RI: 3.90-4.90 [3.90-4.90]), and moderate hyperglycemia (10.8 mmol/L [194 mg/dL]; RI: 3.6-6.2 [64.86-111.71]). Treatment with IV calcium gluconate 10% (0.5 mL/kg over 10 min twice) resolved signs and normalized iCa (1.20 mmol/L [4.8 mg/dL]). Isotonic crystalloids with potassium and maropitant were given for hydration, electrolyte correction, and nausea. Oral calcium (60 mg/kg, q 24 h) was started on Day 1; iCa remained normal (1.26 mmol/L [5.04 mg/dL]) at Day 2, and the kitten was discharged. records.title: More than a scratch, Capnocytophaga bacteremia induced severe sepsis with multi-organ failure with occupational dog exposure: A case report.
records.abstract: Capnocytophaga  species are fastidious gram-negative bacilli found in the oral flora of dogs and cats. Although human infection is typically associated with localized soft tissue disease following animal exposure, invasive infection can result in severe sepsis. We present a case of  Capnocytophaga  bacteremia in an immunocompetent woman with occupational exposure to dogs. A 49-year-old woman with a history of Factor V Leiden mutation, prior deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and Raynaud's syndrome presented with fever, chills, fatigue, myalgias, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and transient vaginal bleeding. Evaluation revealed acute kidney injury, lactic acidosis, transaminitis, severe thrombocytopenia, and a petechial rash. An extensive infectious and autoimmune workup was unrevealing. Further history revealed recurrent occupational exposure to dogs as a photographer and walker, including a recent healing scratch to her right arm without evidence of local infection. Due to persistent leukocytosis and lack of clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was escalated to meropenem, resulting in gradual clinical and laboratory recovery. Blood cultures eventually grew  Capnocytophaga  species after delayed growth on anaerobic media. The patient was transitioned to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate to complete a two-week course. Susceptibility testing could not be performed because of insufficient organism growth. This case highlights the potential for severe  Capnocytophaga  bacteremia in an immunocompetent host with recurrent occupational exposure to animals. The nonspecific presentation and difficulty identifying this fastidious organism contributed to diagnostic uncertainty and delayed targeted therapy. Clinicians should consider  Capnocytophaga  infection in patients with unexplained sepsis and a history of animal exposure, even in the absence of a significant bite wound or overt soft-tissue infection.

records.title: Ovarian leiomyoma with an epithelioid differentiation in a dog.

records.abstract: A 12-years-3-months-old female Toy Poodle underwent ovariohysterectomy, and an 8-mm ovarian mass was incidentally identified on pathological examination. records.title: Histological and proteomic characterization of hyaline material in two dogs with hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
records.journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
records.abstract: Hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinoma is a rare subtype of exocrine pancreatic carcinoma in dogs, characterized by abundant extracellular hyaline material within the tumor. In this study, we investigated two canine cases exhibiting this distinctive hyalinizing morphology using histological, proteomic, immunohistochemical, ultrastructural, and molecular approaches. Histological examination revealed amyloid-like eosinophilic hyaline deposits; however, these deposits lacked diagnostic features of amyloid, as confirmed by Congo red and thioflavin S staining and transmission electron microscopy. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) identified bile salt-activated lipase (BAL) as the predominant component of the hyaline deposits. Immunohistochemistry confirmed strong anti-BAL immunoreactivity in the deposits. In addition to BAL, amyloid-associated proteins, including clusterin, vitronectin, apolipoprotein E, and apolipoprotein A-I, were detected. Together with the negative Congo red and thioflavin S staining and ultrastructural findings, these results support that the hyaline deposits are BAL-rich, non-amyloid extracellular deposits. Some deposits also contained collagen, indicating biochemical heterogeneity of the hyaline material. RT-qPCR analysis suggested higher CEL, and lower GRP94 expression in hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinomas than in non-hyalinizing pancreatic carcinomas. These observations raise a hypothesis that excessive BAL production, together with reduced GRP94-mediated chaperone support, may contribute to extracellular accumulation of aggregated BAL. Collectively, this study identifies BAL as the predominant component of hyaline deposits in canine hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinoma based on LC-MS/MS analysis and highlights a non-amyloid protein aggregation process associated with this tumor subtype.

records.title: A dog with suspected hypothalamic hypoadrenocorticism classified by corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) testing.
records.journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
records.abstract: A 7-year-old intact male toy poodle presented with abdominal distension, polydipsia, and polyuria. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed bilateral adrenal atrophy, and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation testing showed persistently low cortisol concentrations with concurrent low endogenous ACTH, indicating central hypoadrenocorticism. To localize dysfunction within the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, a corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulation test was performed. Endogenous ACTH increased markedly after CRH administration, whereas cortisol remained undetectable, demonstrating preserved pituitary responsiveness and supporting a diagnosis of hypothalamic hypoadrenocorticism. Treatment of hypoadrenocorticism with prednisolone alone resulted in long-term clinical stabilization without electrolyte abnormalities for over one year. To our knowledge, this is the first canine report classifying suspected hypothalamic hypoadrenocorticism using CRH stimulation testing.

records.title: Esophageal strictures associated with prolonged nasoesophageal tube placement in three cats.
records.abstract: Nasoesophageal tube placement for a prolonged period of time has not previously been associated with esophageal stricture in cats. Three cats with suspected hepatic lipidosis required extended enteral nutritional support because voluntary food intake remained < 25% of the calculated resting energy requirement. The cumulative duration of nasoesophageal tube placement was 24-37 days. Regurgitation or retching developed within 1-3 days after tube removal, and esophagoscopy identified severe focal strictures in the cervical esophagus at the C4-C6 vertebral level in all 3 cats. One cat underwent 3 endoscopic balloon dilatation sessions at 1-week intervals, with enlargement of the esophageal lumen. The consistent anatomic location and temporal association with prolonged tube placement suggest that extended nasoesophageal intubation may be a risk factor for cervical esophageal stricture formation in cats. When prolonged nutritional support is anticipated, transition to a feeding tube intended for long-term use should be considered.

records.title: Concurrent Pericardial Effusion Leading to Cardiac Tamponade as the Initial Manifestation of Multicentric Lymphoma in a Dog.
records.abstract: Multicentric lymphoma is one of the most common haematopoietic neoplasms in dogs and may present with variable systemic and cardiothoracic manifestations. This report describes a case of multicentric lymphoma in an 8-year-old mixed-breed dog presenting with severe respiratory distress associated with concurrent pleural and pericardial effusions leading to cardiac tamponade. Clinical investigation included thoracic radiography, abdominal ultrasonography, echocardiography, electrocardiography and cytological evaluation of pericardial fluid. Imaging examinations revealed marked cardiomegaly, hepatomegaly, splenic mass and significant thoracic effusions associated with cardiopulmonary compromise. Pericardiocentesis was performed as both therapeutic and diagnostic procedure, allowing temporary haemodynamic stabilization and cytological identification of malignant lymphoid proliferation compatible with multicentric lymphoma. Despite supportive treatment and transient clinical improvement, rapid recurrence of respiratory signs resulted in death. This report highlights the clinical importance of recognizing concurrent thoracic effusions as potential indicators of advanced systemic neoplasia in dogs. The case emphasizes the value of rapid multimodal diagnostic investigation, particularly the integration of imaging techniques and cavitary fluid cytology, in the management of critically ill patients with suspected neoplastic thoracic disease.

records.title: Suspected Anaphylactoid Reaction Induced by Intravenous Propofol Administration in a Dog.
records.abstract: This report describes a case of suspected peri-induction hypersensitivity reaction associated with propofol administration in a dog. A 14-month-old female Shih-Tzu underwent anaesthetic induction with propofol and lidocaine for elective ovariohysterectomy. Shortly after induction, the patient developed severe hypotension refractory to fluid therapy and dobutamine, followed by cardiopulmonary arrest. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was successfully performed. Post-resuscitation findings included marked gallbladder wall thickening and transient free peritoneal fluid on ultrasonography, as well as a marked increase in alanine aminotransferase activity. Supportive care, including vasopressor therapy and corticosteroid administration, resulted in progressive hemodynamic and biochemical recovery. A suspected hypersensitivity reaction temporally associated with anaesthetic induction was considered the most likely differential diagnosis. However, alternative mechanisms such as post-arrest hypoperfusion and venous congestion could not be excluded. This report highlights the diagnostic challenges in distinguishing hypersensitivity reactions from other causes of acute hemodynamic instability.

records.title: Milk-related food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis with suspected pork-cat syndrome in an 11-year-old boy.
records.abstract: Pork-cat syndrome (PCS) is caused by cross-reactivity between cat serum albumin (Fel d 2) and pork serum albumin (Sus s 1). Although bovine serum albumin (Bos d 6) is also homologous to Fel d 2, milk-related symptoms have rarely been described in patients with PCS. We report an 11-year-old boy with food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis (FDEIA) in whom milk was identified as the trigger and serum albumin cross-reactivity was suspected as a possible mechanism. He had experienced two episodes of anaphylaxis after eating pork sausage for breakfast and school lunch containing milk and pork, followed by exercise. He had lived with a cat since birth. Serum testing showed high levels of specific IgE to Fel d 2, Sus s 1, Bos d 6, cat dander, pork, beef, and milk, whereas casein-specific and alpha-gal-specific IgE levels were low. Skin prick testing was positive for raw pork, raw beef, pork sausage, and unheated milk, but negative for heated pork, heated beef, and heated milk. In an oral food challenge, symptoms were reproduced after exercise following ingestion of 300 mL of unheated milk, leading to a diagnosis of milk-related FDEIA. Inhibition enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay demonstrated partial inhibition of IgE reactivity to Bos d 6 by pork, cat hair, and milk extracts at the tested concentration. These findings suggested serum albumin cross-reactivity involving PCS. This case highlights the clinical utility of component-resolved diagnosis, particularly low casein-specific IgE with high Bos d 6-specific IgE, in raising suspicion of serum albumin-related mechanisms in patients with milk-related FDEIA.

records.title: Surgical Management of a Testicular Spermatocytic Tumour in a Rescued Snow Leopard (Panthera uncia) With Successful Wild Reintroduction.
records.abstract: Neoplastic diseases in wild felids are rarely documented, particularly in threatened species such as the snow leopard (Panthera uncia). An adult male snow leopard rescued in Qinghai Province, China, presented with severe emaciation and marked scrotal enlargement that restricted normal movement. Bilateral orchiectomy was performed following clinical examination and imaging assessment. Histopathological analysis revealed large round tumour cells with prominent nucleoli and frequent mitotic figures. Immunohistochemical staining supported the diagnosis of a spermatocytic tumour with epididymal involvement. After surgery and postoperative care, the animal gradually recovered body condition. Behavioural evaluation indicated that it retained the ability to survive independently in the wild. The individual was therefore released after rehabilitation. Satellite tracking recorded normal movement patterns and confirmed survival for at least 3 years following release. This report provides clinical and pathological documentation of a testicular spermatocytic tumour in a snow leopard and indicates that surgical intervention may be feasible in selected cases encountered during wildlife rescue.

records.title: Adjuvant Interstitial Yttrium-90 Hydrogel (IsoPet ® ) Following Limb-Sparing Marginal Excision of Multifocal Distal Pelvic-Limb Neoplasia in a Dog.
records.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
records.abstract: Achieving complete surgical margins can be challenging for tumors involving the distal extremities due to limited surrounding soft tissue and the proximity of functionally important structures. Incompletely excised tumors may require adjuvant radiation therapy to treat suspected residual microscopic disease. Yttrium-90 phosphate hydrogel (IsoPet ® ) is an emerging injectable radiation modality that delivers localized beta radiation to a tumor bed or surgical margin. An eight-year-old neutered male Bullmastiff was evaluated by the referring veterinarian for firm subcutaneous masses developed along the right pelvic limb. Fine-needle aspiration was initially suggestive of an inflammatory process; however, subsequent punch biopsies identified Grade II soft tissue sarcoma. The patient was referred for surgical oncology evaluation. Four right pelvic limb masses and the right popliteal lymph node were surgically excised. Histopathological examination of the excisional specimens identified poorly differentiated carcinoma involving the excised masses, with metastatic involvement of the right popliteal lymph node and incomplete surgical margins. Adjuvant Y-90 hydrogel was elected following complete surgical wound healing. On 20 November 2025, 8.46 mCi (313 MBq) of Y-90 phosphate hydrogel in a total volume of 4.7 mL was administered through 66 peri-incisional and incisional injections distributed across the previous right pelvic limb surgical beds using a grid-based technique. The procedure was completed without complications. Post-treatment follow-up demonstrated satisfactory wound healing, with only mild transient appetite reduction and minimal localized tissue irritation. After surgery plus adjuvant Y-90, no clinically detectable local recurrence was identified at the treatment sites during the 120-day documented follow-up period. Seventy-four days following Y-90 hydrogel treatment, computed tomography performed for persistent otic disease identified an aggressive osteolytic lesion involving the right C5 vertebra with extradural spinal cord compression. The relationship between this lesion and the previously treated pelvic limb neoplasia could not be definitively established. Despite the subsequent development of this cervical lesion, no clinically detectable recurrence was documented at the original treatment limb sites. This finding is an observation after combined surgery and Y-90, not evidence of Y-90-specific efficacy. The patient was subsequently managed supportively and was euthanized by the referring veterinarian approximately four months after identification of the cervical lesion. This single case demonstrates that peri-incisional Y-90 phosphate hydrogel could be administered to multiple distal pelvic-limb surgical beds after limb-sparing excision. The procedure was well tolerated. No clinically detectable local recurrence was identified at the treated sites during the 120-day documented follow-up period. Because gross disease had already been removed and there was no comparator, these observations cannot establish the independent efficacy of IsoPet ® . Prospective studies are needed.

records.title: Acute Levothyroxine Overdose Followed by Serial Monitoring of Total Thyroxine and Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone in a Hypothyroid Dog.
records.abstract: Reports of acute levothyroxine overdose in dogs are rare with limited monitoring data. An 8-year-old spayed female Pomeranian receiving long-term hypothyroidism treatment presented 9 h after ingesting a one-month supply of levothyroxine (3 mg; 1.13 mg/kg). Except for transient tachycardia, the physical examination revealed unremarkable findings. The total thyroxine (T4) level exceeded the upper limit of quantification. These findings suggest that acute overdose is less severe than chronic levothyroxine exposure.

records.title: Chronic Recurrent Septic Peritonitis in a Diabetic Dog Caused by Staphylococcus pseudintermedius With Splendore-Hoeppli Reaction (Botryomycosis-Like/Bacterial Pseudomycetoma).
records.abstract: A 6-year-old neutered male Miniature Pinscher with poorly regulated diabetes mellitus was evaluated for recurrent abdominal effusion, lethargy and inappetence secondary to chronic septic peritonitis. Across four discrete clinical episodes, Staphylococcus pseudintermedius was repeatedly isolated in pure culture from peritoneal fluid and omental tissue, with consistent antimicrobial susceptibility profiles across submissions, a pattern suggestive of strain persistence rather than serial reinfection. Histopathology of omental biopsies demonstrated severe, chronic pyogranulomatous peritonitis with prominent Splendore-Hoeppli material surrounding bacterial colonies, consistent with bacterial pseudomycetoma. Despite two exploratory laparotomies with extensive abdominal lavage, closed-suction peritoneal drainage, broad-spectrum systemic antimicrobial therapy, and a subsequent salvage protocol of combined intravenous and intraperitoneal meropenem administered via an ultrasound-guided peritoneal catheter, infection ultimately recurred and the dog was humanely euthanized. records.title: Chemodectoma Arising From the Abdominal Aorta in a 9-Year-Old Female Dog: Clinical, Histopathological and Immunohistochemstric Study.
records.abstract: Chemodectomas are uncommon, typically benign neoplasms derived from paraganglionic chemoreceptor tissues, most frequently arising in the heart base or carotid bodies of brachycephalic dogs. This report documents a detailed pathological description of a chemodectoma originating from the abdominal aorta in a non-human species, representing, to our knowledge, the first case specifically characterized by its origin at the aortic trifurcation, thereby expanding the recognized anatomical spectrum of this tumour entity. A 9-year-old spayed female terrier was presented with persistent panting, recent-onset obesity following previous cachexia, and a complex clinical history including polyuria/polydipsia and pyoderma. Haematological and biochemical analyses revealed a regenerative anaemia, leucocytosis, and biochemical indicators suggestive of cholestasis and potential endocrinopathy. Advanced imaging identified a solitary, well-demarcated, highly vascular abdominal mass closely associated with the aortic trifurcation. Given the tumour's inaccessibility and pronounced vascularity, cytological confirmation via fine needle aspiration was precluded due to haemorrhagic risk, necessitating exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperatively, the mass was unresectable because of its anatomical relationships and the prohibitive risk of catastrophic haemorrhage. Humane euthanasia was subsequently elected. Histopathological evaluation demonstrated a lobulated neoplasm composed of pleomorphic neuroendocrine cells, with low mitotic activity and an absence of necrosis or haemorrhage. Immunohistochemistry confirmed strong, diffuse synaptophysin reactivity and focal neuron-specific enolase positivity, while chromogranin A and S100 protein were negative, underscoring immunophenotypic variability. This case illustrates the diagnostic complexity and therapeutic limitations posed by extra-cardiac chemodectomas in veterinary species, especially when located in unconventional anatomical sites. Limitations included the unavailability of computed tomography and lack of postoperative follow-up. This report expands the recognized clinico-pathological spectrum of chemodectomas and highlights the necessity for multidisciplinary diagnostic strategies and further research aimed at defining optimal management protocols for such rare and challenging presentations.

records.title: Primary Erythrocytosis (Polycythaemia) in a Neutered Male Dog Presenting With Right Hindlimb Lameness.
records.abstract: A 2-year-old male entire Cocker Spaniel was referred for investigation of progressive right hindlimb lameness and polyuria and polydipsia. Investigations conducted by the primary care veterinary surgeon revealed erythrocytosis (haematocrit of 78%, reference interval: 37%-55%) and urine concentration consistent with polyuria and polydipsia (specific gravity 1.014). Upon referral, physical examination revealed a dark red oral mucosa and right hindlimb lameness, characterised by intermittent non-weight bearing of the limb when standing. Neurological examination only revealed a mild short-strided gait, and orthopaedic examination was unremarkable. Secondary causes of erythrocytosis were excluded by normal arterial blood gas, low erythropoietin levels and normal thoracic and abdominal imaging, resulting in a diagnosis of primary erythrocytosis (PE). Focal ultrasonography identified a right external iliac venous thrombus, suspected to be the cause of the right hindlimb lameness and presumed to be associated with the PE. Initial management involved repeated phlebotomies, followed by long-term treatment with hydroxyurea (31 mg/kg twice weekly) and rivaroxaban (2 mg/kg once daily). At the 5-month recheck, the dog was asymptomatic, with resolution of the iliac thrombus and a normal haematocrit. This case highlights an unusual presentation of PE in a dog, not previously described in the veterinary literature, and re-examines the discussion on the optimal management of this rare condition, with a focus on the necessity of antithrombotic therapy.

records.title: Unilateral Hormonally Active Testicular Sertoli Cell Tumour and Feminization Syndrome in a Bernese Mountain Dog With Normally Descended Testes.
records.abstract: To describe the clinical presentation, diagnostic workup and successful outcome of a hormonally active testicular Sertoli cell tumour (SCT) in a non-cryptorchid Bernese Mountain Dog. A 10-year-old intact male dog was evaluated with a history of progressive alopecia, gynaecomastia and haematuria. Diagnostic investigations included complete blood count, serum biochemistry, oestradiol assay, abdominal and testicular ultrasonography, preputial cytology and histopathological examination following bilateral orchiectomy. Clinical signs included bilaterally symmetrical alopecia, hyperpigmentation and a pendulous prepuce. Laboratory findings revealed mild non-regenerative anaemia and severe hyperestrogenism (oestradiol: 119 pg/mL). Preputial cytology showed a predominance of superficial epithelial cells (> 80%), supporting the state of hyperestrogenism. Ultrasonography identified a large, vascularized left testicular mass and cystic prostatic changes. Histopathology confirmed an SCT. Following surgery, clinical signs and laboratory abnormalities resolved completely within 9 months. This case emphasizes that SCTs should be a differential diagnosis for feminization syndrome in older dogs even without cryptorchidism. It also highlights preputial cytology as a rapid and effective minimally invasive tool for the preliminary identification of hyperestrogenism.

records.title: Intraoperative Indocyanine Green Fluorescence for Assessment of Suspected Venous Invasion in a Dog With Thyroid Carcinoma.
records.abstract: Accurate intraoperative assessment of vascular involvement in canine thyroid carcinoma remains challenging when preoperative imaging findings are equivocal. This case describes the use of intraoperative indocyanine green fluorescence imaging to assist real-time assessment of suspected venous involvement during canine thyroidectomy. A 5-year-old spayed female Maltese dog was presented with a cervical mass and clinicopathological findings consistent with hypothyroidism. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography identified a left thyroid mass with suspected external jugular vein compression but no definitive evidence of vascular invasion. During left thyroidectomy, dilation and distal tapering of the thyroid veins raised concern for venous involvement. Indocyanine green (0.5 mg/dog) was administered intravenously for intraoperative near-infrared fluorescence imaging. Diffuse fluorescence of the thyroid mass and segmental intraluminal fluorescence within the dilated thyroid vein were observed, with signal loss at the tapering point. Based on these findings, en bloc resection including a short segment of the involved vein was performed. Histopathology confirmed thyroid carcinoma without evidence of regional lymph node metastasis. This case illustrates that intraoperative indocyanine green fluorescence imaging may provide adjunctive real-time information for assessing suspected venous involvement during canine thyroid carcinoma surgery and may complement preoperative imaging when vascular invasion is uncertain.

records.title: Carotid body carcinoma in a French bulldog treated with toceranib phosphate.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: Carotid body tumors are rare neuroendocrine neoplasms in dogs, and evidence-based treatment options for malignant or unresectable cases remain poorly defined. An 8-year-old castrated male French bulldog was presented with a large cervical mass accompanied by progressive respiratory distress, neurologic abnormalities, and exophthalmos. Computed tomography revealed multiple, highly vascularized cervical masses with extensive local invasion, including nasopharyngeal obstruction and intracranial extension. Partial surgical excision was undertaken for diagnostic purposes, and histopathologic examination confirmed carotid body carcinoma with intravascular invasion. Because of incomplete surgical resection and malignant features, targeted therapy was initiated. Based on  in vitro  chemosensitivity testing, toceranib phosphate was selected. Following treatment, clinical signs related to mass effect improved, nasopharyngeal obstruction was alleviated, and increased intratumoral necrosis was suspected on follow-up imaging. Adverse effects were mild and manageable. The dog remained clinically stable for ~5 mo after targeted therapy but was subsequently lost to follow-up. On a later follow-up  via  telephone, the owner reported that the dog had died 6 mo after initiation of targeted therapy. Key clinical message: This case suggests that toceranib may represent a potential therapeutic option for dogs with unresectable or incompletely resected carotid body carcinoma.

records.title: Clinical and  18 F-FDG PET/CT imaging features in a dog with bacterial sepsis of unknown origin.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: Positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18] fluoro-D-glucose integrated with computed tomography ( 18 F-FDG PET/CT) imaging identified infection and inflammation earlier and with higher sensitivity than other imaging modalities in human medicine. A small case series explored the use of  18 F-FDG PET/CT for detecting the cause of fever of unknown origin in dogs. This report details clinical aspects and  18 F-FDG PET/CT imaging in the workup and treatment of a 12-year-old dog that was presented obtunded with severe neutropenia and hypoglycemia secondary to suspected sepsis. The  18 F-FDG PET/CT revealed moderate, patchy FDG avidity and soft-tissue swelling of the left carpus and tarsus (SUV max: 7.18 and SUV max: 5.58, respectively), moderate heterogeneous splenic and hepatic hypermetabolic activity (SUV max: 3.42), and bilaterally symmetric renal hypermetabolic activity (SUV max: 6.22) without appropriate flourine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18 F-FDG) excretion. Other notable findings included marked, diffuse  18 F-FDG uptake within all bone marrow spaces (SUV max: 15.47) and a generalized, mild lymphadenopathy with moderate hypermetabolic activity. Positive blood cultures confirmed sepsis. Clinical deterioration despite appropriate antibiotic and supportive therapy prompted euthanasia. Necropsy revealed lymphohistiocytic and neutrophilic necrotizing vasculitis with thrombosis and necrosis in heart, spleen, brain, and liver, consistent with septicemia.  Enterococcus faecium  was isolated from lungs, kidneys, and spleen;  Serratia marcescens  was isolated from lungs and kidneys. This is the first documented report of the use of  18 F-FDG PET/CT for the diagnostic workup of a septic patient in veterinary medicine with corroborative necropsy findings to confirm PET/CT suspicion of disseminated septicemia. Key clinical message: Positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18] fluoro-D-glucose integrated with computed tomography imaging, which combines the functional, metabolic information from a PET scan with the high-resolution anatomical detail from a CT scan, should be considered as an adjunctive imaging modality for the diagnostic workup to identify focal and systemic infections in veterinary medicine. This is critical for immunocompromised animals in which timely and accurate diagnosis is of utmost importance, either for guiding case management and clinical outcome or for guiding owners through difficult decisions when the prognosis is guarded to poor.

records.title: Ultrasonographic features and clinical outcome of an anaplastic carcinoma arising from a uterus masculinus in an intact, non-cryptorchid male dog.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: A 6-year-old intact male dog was referred because of persistent hematuria despite multiple courses of antimicrobial therapy. Urogenital ultrasonography revealed a large, paraprostatic, uterus-like, fluid-filled structure containing echogenic fluid, associated with an adjacent large, heterogeneous mass located cranially and to the right of the lesion. These findings raised suspicion for malignant transformation of a uterus masculinus associated with persistent Müllerian duct syndrome. Exploratory laparotomy confirmed the presence of a uterus masculinus with blind-ended uterine horns, associated adhesions, and a large mass arising from the right cranial aspect. Surgical excision of the abnormal structure and orchiectomy were carried out. Histopathology confirmed an anaplastic carcinoma of Müllerian origin arising from persistent Müllerian duct remnants. The tumor exhibited highly aggressive biological behavior characterized by extensive local invasion. There was rapid clinical deterioration after surgery, including imaging findings consistent with pulmonary, hepatic, and peritoneal metastatic disease, ultimately leading to euthanasia 5 wk after diagnosis. Key clinical message: Persistent Müllerian duct remnants should be considered as a differential diagnosis for paraprostatic cavitary lesions in intact male dogs, even in the absence of cryptorchidism. Malignant transformation of a uterus masculinus, though rare, may exhibit highly aggressive biological behavior with rapid metastatic dissemination.

records.title: Treatment of Refractory Vomiting With Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine in Two Dogs and a Cat: A Cases Series.
records.abstract: Refractory vomiting in dogs and cats is a common clinical condition in small animal practice, typically characterized by recurrent vomiting, belching and related symptoms, which is a great challenge to veterinarians. According to Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine (TCVM), this condition is primarily attributed to dysfunction of the spleen and stomach in transformation and transportation, leading to the upward rebellion of stomach Qi. Derived from the Shang Han Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage), Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction functions to direct rebellious Qi downward, resolve phlegm, tonify Qi and harmonize the stomach. It is mainly indicated for conditions resulting from stomach Qi counter flow. In this report, three cases of refractory vomiting in two dogs and a cat diagnosed as stomach Qi rebellion according to TCVM were treated with modified Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction based on syndrome differentiation. The results showed that all three cases achieved favourable therapeutic outcomes. These findings suggest that, for refractory vomiting caused by stomach Qi rebellion in dogs and cats, individualized treatment with modified Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction based on specific clinical presentations can achieve stable and reliable efficacy.

records.title: Novel Therapy for Severe Bilateral Pyogranulomatous Blepharitis Secondary to Hyaluronic Acid Filler in a Dog.
records.abstract: A 9-year-old female spayed mixed breed dog was initially examined for severe bilateral entropion secondary to enophthalmos from chronic oral steroid use for immune-mediated thrombocytopenia as well as potential historic masticatory muscle myositis. Surgical intervention with entropion surgery was pursued; however, trichiasis secondary to laxity of the periocular muscles, eyelid tissues, and tarsal plate developed several months later. Hyaluronic acid (HA) filler (Alayna SG 24 Distinct, BSC Medical Devices GmbH, Munich, Germany) was injected into the superior and inferior eyelids of both eyes to correct recurrent ocular irritation. One month later, the patient developed severe, presumed pyogranulomatous blepharitis in both eyes suspected to be a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to the HA filler. The condition worsened despite medical management. Due to the patient's previous, chronic history of oral steroid use, the owners declined administration of oral steroids at that time. Oral Zenrelia (ilunocitinib) and topical neomycin-polymyxin-dexamethasone ointment were instituted, which resulted in a rapid resolution of the patient's clinical signs. This is the first known report of a dog experiencing a severe hypersensitivity reaction to hyaluronic acid used as an eyelid filler and successful treatment with Zenrelia for this purpose.

records.title: Removal of a lodged endotracheal tube in an anaesthetised French Bulldog using manual laryngeal stabilisation and neuromuscular blockade, and subsequent complications.
records.abstract: A 5-year-old, female neutered French Bulldog presented under anaesthesia with an endotracheal tube (ETT) lodged in the larynx. Cuff inflation and deflation, application of lubricant, ETT rotation, and repeated traction did not allow ETT removal. The ETT was successfully removed under neuromuscular blockade with manual laryngeal stabilisation: the left thumb pressed against the epiglottis intraorally and the left index and middle fingers gripped the larynx externally to immobilise the larynx. The right-hand applied traction to the ETT, which could then be extracted. The dog's larynx obstructed on recovery from anaesthesia with suspected temporary laryngeal paralysis. The dog was managed with a tracheostomy tube for 3 days and made a good recovery. The dog presented in respiratory distress 4 weeks later with tracheal stenosis that was successfully treated with tracheal resection and anastomosis. This case report describes the use of neuromuscular blockade and manual laryngeal stabilisation to remove a lodged ETT and reflects on the subsequent complications.

records.title: Rare Feline Gingival Extramedullary Plasmacytoma: Clinical Application of Electrochemotherapy for Local Control.
records.abstract: Feline extramedullary plasmacytoma (EMP) is an uncommon plasma cell neoplasm typically regarded as biologically benign; however, its clinical behaviour may be heterogeneous. This case report describes an aggressive gingival EMP in a 14-year-old neutered male Turkish Angora cat, characterised by alveolar bone lysis and cytologically confirmed regional lymph node metastasis in the absence of systemic features consistent with multiple myeloma. Histopathological examination revealed an infiltrative round cell neoplasm with high mitotic index, and strong diffuse MUM-1 immunoreactivity confirmed the diagnosis. As complete surgical excision was declined, and tumour regrowth occurred after repeated radiation therapy, electrochemotherapy (ECT) was selected for local tumour control. Bleomycin (15,000 IU/m 2  IV) was administered before pulse delivery, and three ECT sessions were performed at weekly intervals. The tumour volume decreased by more than 70%, which was consistent with a partial response, and only mild self-limiting local adverse effects were observed. No systemic toxicity was observed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report describing the use of ECT for feline gingival EMP. This case highlights the potential biological heterogeneity of feline EMP and suggests that ECT may provide short-term local tumour reduction and palliation when complete surgical excision is not feasible.

records.abstract: A 3-year-old neutered male Siamese cat with chronic anorexia showed anemia and elevated liver enzyme levels. records.title: Spontaneous Reduction in Mitral Valve Regurgitation in Three Dogs With Severe Myxomatous Mitral Valve Disease: An Unusual Case Report.
records.abstract: Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD), the most common heart disease in small-breed dogs, is characterized by mitral regurgitation (MR) resulting from valvular degeneration, which may progress to left-sided heart failure. This report describes the cases of three dogs with severe MMVD (American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine Stages C or D) who exhibited an unexpected spontaneous reduction in MR despite continued valve degeneration. Three dogs initially presented with symptoms of heart failure and left atrial and ventricular enlargement. Standard treatment, including diuretics, improved their conditions; however, further monitoring revealed that the coaptation gap decreased due to mitral valve thickening, leading to a reduction in MR. This was accompanied by a significant decrease in heart size. As a result, diuretics were discontinued, and all dogs were successfully managed with pimobendan alone. To our knowledge, this is the first report of spontaneous MR reduction in MMVD, where coaptation gap narrowing played a role in clinical improvement. These cases may broaden the current understanding of MMVD progression, suggesting that, in rare instances, changes in cardiac remodelling and clinical status can occur. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms.

records.title: Left Medial Liver Lobe Torsion Associated With Hepatocellular Carcinoma in a Pembroke Welsh Corgi: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Liver lobe torsion (LLT) is a rare, potentially life-threatening condition in dogs and is reported most often in medium- to large-breed dogs. Neoplasia-associated LLT is unusual, and detailed descriptions of LLT associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) are scarce. A 12-year-old spayed female Pembroke Welsh Corgi (9.5 kg) presented with acute collapse after several months of progressive lethargy and inappetence. Laboratory abnormalities included increased alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase activities and C-reactive protein concentration. Computed tomography (CT) identified a 7.2 × 6.7 × 6.5 cm mass arising from the left medial liver lobe, a whirl sign at the base of the mass and a non-enhancing hypoattenuating region consistent with necrosis. Midline celiotomy and left medial liver lobectomy were performed without detorsion. Cytology of abdominal effusion was consistent with a culture-negative inflammatory exudate. Histopathology confirmed HCC with extensive necrosis, and the examined surgical margin was free of neoplastic cells. The dog recovered uneventfully, was discharged on postoperative Day 4 and had no recurrence of clinical abnormalities at 1-year follow-up. This case highlights the apparent association between HCC and LLT and the unusual location of the torsion axis at the base of the mass rather than at the hepatic hilus, although causality cannot be established from a single case. CT visualisation of the whirl sign at this atypical site was instrumental in establishing the preoperative diagnosis and guiding surgical planning.

records.title: Bilateral Keratouveitis and Secondary Glaucoma in a Young Dog With Immune-Mediated Polyarthritis and Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome.
records.abstract: A 7-month-old intact female mixed-breed dog presented emergently for inability to walk, lethargy, and vomiting. The patient was diagnosed with immune-mediated polyarthritis (IMPA) and secondary systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Bilateral keratouveitis and secondary glaucoma developed within 24 h of presentation. Thorough diagnostic testing failed to identify an underlying etiology. Despite aggressive medical management, the patient developed rapid vision loss. Due to poor visual prognosis and anticipated need for long-term medical management, both eyes were enucleated. Histopathological evaluation of both globes revealed severe corneal endothelial injury most consistent with endotheliitis with associated uveitis and endophthalmitis. Testing of ocular tissue with PCR and immunohistochemistry for canine adenovirus was negative, and comprehensive infectious disease screening, joint cultures, and ocular histopathology identified no other causative agents. Following enucleation, the dog systemically improved with anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial medical management. This report highlights a unique and severe case of bilateral keratouveitis with glaucoma following a systemic inflammatory event.

records.title: Anterior Segment OCT Diagnosis of Descemet's Membrane Detachment in a Cat With Suspected FIP-Associated Uveitis.
records.abstract: Persistent corneal edema in cats with anterior uveitis is often attributed to endothelial dysfunction; however, the underlying structural cause may not be apparent without advanced imaging. Descemet's membrane detachment (DMD) is rarely reported in cats and has not been well described in suspected feline infectious peritonitis (FIP)-associated uveitis. A 4-month-old intact male Norwegian Forest cat presented with severe unilateral granulomatous uveitis, mutton-fat keratic precipitates, diffuse stromal edema, and a 2+ aqueous flare. Aqueous humor PCR detected feline coronavirus RNA, although biotype testing did not confirm a mutation consistent with that associated with feline infectious peritonitis virus. As ocular inflammation progressed despite anti-inflammatory treatment, the nucleoside analog GS-441524 was administered along with anti-inflammatory and supportive ophthalmic treatment. Intraocular inflammation improved, but corneal edema persisted, prompting anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT), which revealed planar DMD. Serial AS-OCT monitored posterior corneal structural changes. Corneal edema gradually decreased, and Descemet's membrane reapposition was documented by AS-OCT approximately one year after the initial presentation. Corneal clarity and stability were maintained without clinically evident recurrence for 18 months after reapposition was confirmed. This case describes the AS-OCT diagnosis and serial documentation of DMD and subsequent Descemet's membrane reapposition in a cat with suspected FIP-associated uveitis. These findings highlight the value of AS-OCT for identifying and monitoring posterior corneal abnormalities, including DMD, in cats with severe anterior uveitis and persistent corneal edema. The relationships among suspected FIP-associated uveitis, treatment, and DMD could not be determined from this single case.
